question: Tell me about a time you failed or made a significant mistake. What did you learn and what changed afterward?

raiseTranscript.text: I missed a deadline on a feature flag rollout because I underestimated testing time. I owned it in the retro, asked my mentor for help on estimation, and started breaking tasks into smaller chunks with buffer time.
What specifically changed in how you work now?
I now share rough estimates with the team two days earlier and flag risks in standup. My last two tasks shipped on time.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you failed or made a significant mistake. What did you learn and what changed afterward?
Missed feature flag deadline due to poor testing estimate
Owned it in retro, asked mentor for help on estimation
Quote: "I now share rough estimates two days earlier and flag risks in standup"
Follow-up: What specifically changed? -> Smaller tasks + early risk flagging, last two tasks on time
junior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar on Resilience. Candidate described missing a deadline on a feature flag rollout, immediately owned the miss in the retro, and asked a mentor for help on estimation. They then implemented early risk flagging and smaller task breakdowns, with the concrete outcome that their last two tasks shipped on time. This shows clear coachability and local process change appropriate for a junior scope. The single biggest strength is the direct link from feedback to an observable behavior change rather than just stating a lesson.

lowerTranscript.text: I once deployed code with a bug that caused a small outage. The tests didn't catch it and the requirements were unclear.
What did you personally change after that?
I started double-checking requirements with the PM before starting work.

lowerNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you failed or made a significant mistake. What did you learn and what changed afterward?
Blaming unclear requirements and insufficient tests for the outage
Only change mentioned was double-checking requirements with PM
Quote: "The tests didn't catch it and the requirements were unclear"
Follow-up: What did you personally change? -> Minimal shift, no evidence of deeper reflection or sustained habit
junior.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar on Resilience. The candidate attributed the outage to unclear requirements and insufficient tests without taking ownership of their own estimation or validation gaps. The only change described was a single new step of checking with the PM, which shows limited learning agility. The story stays at the level of external factors rather than demonstrating how the candidate adjusted their own approach after the mistake.

raiseTranscript.text: I led a cross-team migration that caused a two-hour customer impact because we missed a dependency in a downstream service. I ran the post-mortem, took the hit publicly, and worked with the other team to add contract tests.
How did this affect your influence afterward?
Other teams started asking me to review their migration plans early. We reduced similar incidents by 60% over the next quarter.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you failed or made a significant mistake. What did you learn and what changed afterward?
Cross-team migration outage from missed downstream dependency
Owned it publicly, added contract tests with the other team
Quote: "Other teams started asking me to review their migration plans early"
Follow-up: How did this affect your influence? -> 60% reduction in similar incidents next quarter
senior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar on Resilience. The candidate described a cross-team migration outage, publicly owned the miss, and drove the addition of contract tests with the affected team. This led to other teams proactively seeking their input on migrations and a 60% drop in similar incidents. The story demonstrates influence without authority and measurable cross-team impact suitable for senior scope. The biggest strength is the sustained behavior change that extended beyond their own team.

lowerTranscript.text: We had a production issue after a refactor I drove. The rollback took longer than expected.
What changed in how you or the team operate now?
I make sure we have a rollback plan documented before the next change.

lowerNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you failed or made a significant mistake. What did you learn and what changed afterward?
Production issue after refactor with slow rollback
Only change cited was documenting a rollback plan
Quote: "I make sure we have a rollback plan documented before the next change"
Follow-up: What changed in how you or the team operate now? -> No evidence of cross-team learning or broader process shift
senior.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar on Resilience. The candidate described a production issue after a refactor but limited the learning to documenting a rollback plan. There is no sign of cross-team influence or measurable improvement in how the broader group handles changes. The response stays narrowly tactical and does not show the senior-level expectation of raising standards beyond their immediate work.

raiseTranscript.text: My team missed a launch date because two engineers were overloaded. I had not spotted the capacity issue early enough. After the post-mortem I started weekly 1:1 capacity reviews and redistributed work before it became a problem.
How did this affect team outcomes?
Launch reliability improved and the two engineers who were at risk both stayed and later got promoted.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you failed or made a significant mistake. What did you learn and what changed afterward?
Team missed launch due to undetected overload on two engineers
Implemented weekly capacity reviews and redistributed work
Quote: "The two engineers who were at risk both stayed and later got promoted"
Follow-up: How did this affect team outcomes? -> Improved launch reliability and retention/promotion of at-risk engineers
manager.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar on Resilience. The manager described missing a launch because they failed to detect overload on two team members, then introduced weekly capacity reviews and proactive redistribution. The result was better launch reliability plus retention and promotion of the previously overloaded engineers. This shows ownership of team outcomes and development of others, which is core to the manager level. The biggest strength is the direct connection between the failure and a repeatable team process that produced measurable retention gains.

lowerTranscript.text: We missed a deadline because one person on the team dropped the ball.
What did you change in how you manage the team?
I now send more frequent status updates to stakeholders.

lowerNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you failed or made a significant mistake. What did you learn and what changed afterward?
Missed deadline blamed on one team member
Change limited to more frequent stakeholder updates
Quote: "I now send more frequent status updates to stakeholders"
Follow-up: What did you change in how you manage the team? -> No action on team capacity or underperformance handling
manager.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar on Resilience. The candidate attributed the missed deadline to one team member without reflecting on their own role in capacity management or early detection. The only adjustment mentioned was more stakeholder updates, which does not address team development or underperformance. This response lacks the manager-level expectation of creating leverage through better team processes.

raiseTranscript.text: We bet on a new market entry that underperformed by 40% in the first year. I had pushed the board for the investment. We ran a full strategy reset, pivoted the product, and I personally reset expectations with investors.
We now run smaller market tests with clear kill criteria before full bets, and the next two entries met or exceeded targets.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you failed or made a significant mistake. What did you learn and what changed afterward?
40% underperformance on major market entry the candidate had championed
Ran strategy reset, pivoted, reset investor expectations
Quote: "We now run smaller market tests with clear kill criteria before full bets"
Follow-up: What long-term changes resulted? -> Next two entries met targets after new test-and-kill process
exec.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar on Resilience. The executive described a 40% underperformance on a market entry they had personally championed to the board, then led a full strategy reset and investor reset. They institutionalized smaller tests with explicit kill criteria, after which the next two market entries succeeded. This demonstrates strategic judgment under ambiguity and org-level process change. The biggest strength is the translation of a high-stakes failure into a durable decision-making framework that changed how the company allocates capital.

lowerTranscript.text: One of our product lines didn't meet revenue targets. We adjusted the forecast and kept going.
What org-level changes came from that?
We communicate forecasts more conservatively now.

lowerNotes: Q: Tell me about a time you failed or made a significant mistake. What did you learn and what changed afterward?
Product line missed revenue targets
Only change was more conservative forecasting
Quote: "We communicate forecasts more conservatively now"
Follow-up: What org-level changes came from that? -> No evidence of strategic pivots or capital allocation discipline
exec.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar on Resilience. The candidate described a product line missing revenue targets but limited the response to more conservative forecasting. There is no evidence of strategic trade-offs, investor management, or changes to how the organization evaluates bets. This falls short of the executive expectation for long-term thinking and leverage through systemic decision frameworks.
